designers.biography: Italian designer Alessandro Michele became Gucci creative director in 2015, replacing streamlined luxury with an encyclopedic, gender-fluid world of historical reference, romantic eccentricity, and collecting. After leaving Gucci in 2022, he joined Valentino in 2024, translating the Roman house's couture heritage through his personal maximalist and cinematic imagination.

American designer Alexander Wang launched his New York label in 2005, building an influential language of off-duty sportswear, downtown casting, distressed luxury, and nightlife energy. He served as Balenciaga creative director from 2012 to 2015, adapting the house's sculptural archive through technical materials and a restrained contemporary lens.

Chitose Abe (née Sakai) is a Japanese fashion designer and the founder of the luxury label Sacai. Launched in Tokyo in 1999, her brand is globally renowned for its signature "hybrid" aesthetic, which splices contrasting fabrics, utility wear, and classic tailoring into cohesive, multi-dimensional garments.

French couturier Christian Dior founded his Paris house in 1946 and transformed postwar fashion with the sculpted shoulders, narrow waist, and expansive skirts of his 1947 debut. Through a succession of named lines, he continually revised proportion while rebuilding Paris haute couture as an international cultural and commercial force.

London designer Craig Green founded his label in 2012 after completing the Central Saint Martins MA. Beginning with workwear, uniforms, and the worker jacket, he constructs deeply emotional menswear around protection, restraint, vulnerability, ritual, and collective movement. His processions often combine highly wearable garments with sculptural structures that resemble flags, shelters, machines, or devotional objects.

Spanish couturier Cristóbal Balenciaga opened his first house in San Sebastián before establishing his Paris maison in 1937. Celebrated for technical mastery, architectural cutting, and an exact understanding of fabric, he progressively released the body through tunic, sack, baby-doll, and other abstract silhouettes that reshaped twentieth-century couture.

New York designer Dao-Yi Chow co-founded Public School with Maxwell Osborne. Together they developed a distinctly New York approach to sportswear, tailoring, street culture, and uniform, and received major American menswear honors for their work.

Harlem designer Daniel 'Dapper Dan' Day pioneered a luxury streetwear language in the 1980s by translating European fashion symbols through custom garments for hip-hop artists, athletes, and neighborhood clients. His atelier-centered practice joined tailoring, logomania, and cultural authorship, later extending into sanctioned collaborations with Gucci, Gap, and Puma.
Designer and co-founder of Vetements whose career includes creative leadership at Balenciaga and Gucci.
Belgian designer and member of the Antwerp Six, celebrated for sophisticated color, print, textile, and embroidery combinations across menswear and womenswear.

California designer, photographer, filmmaker, and artist Eli Russell Linnetz founded ERL in Venice Beach. His work turns Southern California archetypes—skaters, surfers, prom, Hollywood fantasy, and handcraft—into emotionally heightened fashion images and garments. In 2022 he guest-designed Dior Men's Spring 2023 collection with Kim Jones.

Italian-born Paris couturière Elsa Schiaparelli fused fashion with Surrealism, modern art, wit, and technological experimentation. Working with artists including Salvador Dalí and Jean Cocteau, she organized theatrical thematic collections and used shocking pink, trompe-l'œil, unusual fastenings, and imagery to challenge the boundaries between dress and art.

Russian designer and photographer Gosha Rubchinskiy launched his namesake label in 2008. Drawing on post-Soviet youth culture, skateboarding, uniforms, sportswear, and Cyrillic graphics, his work helped bring a distinctly Russian visual language into international menswear while connecting fashion with photography, film, music, and youth communities.
Founder of Wales Bonner, a label exploring European heritage and Afro-Atlantic cultural traditions.

Colombian-born, Antwerp-trained designer Haider Ackermann launched his namesake label in 2001 and developed a distinctive language of fluid tailoring, rich color, layered draping, and sensual restraint. His career includes creative leadership at Berluti and Tom Ford, as well as a celebrated one-season haute couture collaboration with Jean Paul Gaultier.

Austrian designer Helmut Lang built a radically modern wardrobe from precise tailoring, denim, military utility, technical textiles, and controlled sensuality. After founding his label in Vienna, he moved its center to New York and helped reset the fashion calendar and visual language of the 1990s before leaving fashion in 2005 to pursue art.

Dutch couturier Iris van Herpen founded her Amsterdam-based house in 2007. Her practice combines meticulous handwork with digital fabrication, material science, architecture, dance, and natural systems, producing sculptural garments that test how technology and the living world can reshape the movement and perception of the body.

Japanese designer Issey Miyake founded the Miyake Design Studio in 1970 and built a practice around the relationship between cloth, technology, movement, and everyday life. Rather than treating fashion as surface decoration, he pursued new systems of making—from a single piece of cloth to garment pleating after construction. This profile focuses on work created during Miyake's own design tenure, keeping later collections by Naoki Takizawa, Dai Fujiwara, Yoshiyuki Miyamae, and Satoshi Kondo distinct.

French designer Jean Paul Gaultier launched his label in 1976 and became fashion's enfant terrible through gender-fluid casting, corsetry, Breton stripes, street references, and virtuosic tailoring. He consistently elevated vernacular dress and challenged conventions of age, size, gender, and beauty across ready-to-wear and haute couture.

German designer Jil Sander established her label in Hamburg in 1968 and became one of modern fashion's defining minimalists. Her precise tailoring, luxurious textiles, controlled color, and refusal of ornament reshaped professional dress in the 1980s and 1990s. Sander left and returned to her namesake house several times; this profile attributes only collections from her own creative tenures rather than later work by Raf Simons, Luke and Lucie Meier, or Simone Bellotti.

California-born, Los Angeles-based designer John Elliott founded his namesake label in 2012. Grounded in skate culture, basketball, travel, and intensive fabric development, his work elevates familiar American sportswear through engineered materials, layered proportions, and exacting construction. Elliott debuted on the New York runway for Fall 2015 and has extended the label through womenswear and collaborations with Nike, Converse, Gap, and other performance and streetwear partners.

British fashion designer born in Gibraltar whose career includes his namesake label and creative leadership at Givenchy, Christian Dior, and Maison Margiela. His work is known for narrative-driven collections, historical research, technical cutting, and theatrical presentation.
Founder of JW Anderson whose career includes creative leadership at Loewe and Dior.

Japanese designer Jun Takahashi founded Undercover in 1990 while studying at Bunka Fashion College. Emerging from Harajuku's Ura-Harajuku scene, he fused punk, street culture, fine construction, music, cinema, and emotional storytelling into a practice he describes through the phrase 'We make noise, not clothes.' His work moves between cult graphic garments and highly poetic Paris presentations.
Designer who began his career at Comme des Garçons and launched his namesake line within the house.

Haitian-American designer Kerby Jean-Raymond founded Pyer Moss in New York in 2013. His work uses fashion, music, art, and performance to center Black history and contemporary American life, notably through the three-part American, Also series.

British designer Kim Jones has connected luxury fashion, travel, art collecting, and street culture across his namesake label, Dunhill, Louis Vuitton menswear, Dior Men, and Fendi womenswear and couture. His collaborations—including Supreme at Louis Vuitton and artists at Dior—helped normalize dialogue between heritage houses and contemporary creative communities.
Founder of the McQueen house, known for innovative tailoring and theatrical presentations.

New York-born and Paris-raised creative Luka Sabbat works across fashion, photography, styling, art, and performance. After developing the multimedia project and anti-fashion label Hot Mess with photographer Noah Dillon, he collaborated on clothing, jewelry, and charitable capsules before founding Marking Distance with designer James Pierce. The label transforms Sabbat’s visual travel diary and interests in punk, cinema, uniforms, fetish objects, and distressed vintage clothing into artisanal ready-to-wear.

American designer Marc Jacobs built his career by bringing subculture and historical fashion into luxurious, emotionally direct collections. His 1992 grunge collection for Perry Ellis became a defining rejection of polished convention. He founded his namesake line and served as Louis Vuitton artistic director from 1997 to 2013, establishing its ready-to-wear identity and artist collaborations.

French designer Marine Serre founded her label in 2017 after winning the LVMH Prize. Her crescent-moon second-skin garments, regenerated materials, and hybrid sportswear established a language she calls Futurewear. Sustainability is structural to her practice: discarded household textiles and existing garments become luxury clothing rather than decorative gestures.

Belgian designer Martin Margiela co-founded Maison Martin Margiela with Jenny Meirens in 1988 after working with Jean Paul Gaultier. Through anonymity, collective authorship, exposed construction, replica garments, radical reuse, unusual scale, and the Tabi boot, he changed how fashion understands originality and value. He left his namesake house in 2009; this profile contains only work from his own tenure.

British-Jamaican designer Martine Rose founded her London label in 2007. Her work transforms football culture, rave, reggae, office wear, and masculine archetypes through skewed proportions and intimately chosen locations. Rose has also consulted for Balenciaga menswear and repeatedly reshaped the language of contemporary menswear from an independent position.

American designer Matthew M. Williams founded ALYX—later 1017 ALYX 9SM—in 2015 after work spanning music, performance, and creative direction. His vocabulary joins industrial hardware, utility, subculture, and technical fabrication. Williams served as Givenchy creative director from 2020 through 2023 while continuing his independent label.

French-Belgian designer Matthieu Blazy worked at Raf Simons, Maison Margiela, Céline, Calvin Klein, and Bottega Veneta before becoming Bottega's creative director in 2021. His material illusions and emphasis on movement made craft feel immediate rather than precious. He became artistic director of Chanel fashion activities in 2025, presenting his first ready-to-wear collection for Spring 2026.

New York designer Maxwell Osborne co-founded Public School with Dao-Yi Chow. Their collaborative practice connected precise menswear, athletic references, and the lived visual language of New York, expanding into womenswear and creative leadership at DKNY.
Designer and creative director of Prada and Miu Miu.

Japanese designer and cultural producer Nigo founded A Bathing Ape in 1993 and later Human Made, building an influential bridge among streetwear, vintage Americana, music, collecting, and graphic identity. A co-founder of Billionaire Boys Club, he became artistic director of Kenzo in 2021 and reframed the house through Japanese craft and youth culture.

French designer Olivier Rousteing served as creative director of Balmain from 2011 to 2025. Appointed at 25, he amplified the house's structured glamour through dense embellishment, sharp shoulders, body-conscious silhouettes, and a digitally fluent vision of celebrity and community known as the Balmain Army. His work also brought his mixed-race identity, adoption story, and search for his African heritage into the narrative of a historic Paris house.

American musician, producer, entrepreneur, and designer Pharrell Williams co-founded Billionaire Boys Club and Icecream with Nigo in 2003, bringing music, skateboarding, and Japanese streetwear production into a global lifestyle project. A longtime fashion collaborator, he became Louis Vuitton men's creative director in 2023, using spectacle, community, tailoring, and the house's travel codes to define his tenure.

British designer Phoebe Philo reshaped modern womenswear through influential creative tenures at Chloé and Céline. Her work centers lived experience, autonomy, intelligent proportion, tactile material, and a tension between pragmatism and eccentricity; in 2023 she launched her independent namesake house.

Italian designer Pierpaolo Piccioli joined Valentino in 1999, led accessories with Maria Grazia Chiuri, and became sole creative director in 2016. His couture practice joined saturated color, emotional casting, and historical technique with a broader vision of beauty. After leaving Valentino in 2024, he became creative director of Balenciaga and debuted for Spring 2026.
Belgian fashion designer whose career includes his namesake label and creative leadership roles at Jil Sander, Dior, Calvin Klein, and Prada.

Brooklyn-born Dominican-American designer Raul Lopez is the founder and creative director of Luar. A co-founder of Hood By Air, Lopez launched Luar in 2011 to tell a more personal story shaped by New York's queer underground, his Dominican heritage, family, and the style languages of the city. After periods of hiatus, he returned to New York Fashion Week in 2021 with a sharpened approach to tailoring and accessories, including the instantly recognizable Ana bag. His work turns neighborhood archetypes, glamour, gender performance, and immigrant aspiration into assertive American fashion.
Designer and founder of Comme des Garçons.
California-born designer who founded his independent namesake label in 1994 and later established it in Paris.

British designer and artist Samuel Ross founded A-COLD-WALL* in 2015 after working with Virgil Abloh. His practice examines British class, architecture, industrial materials, and social environments across fashion, objects, and public art.
Fashion designer whose career includes work for Alexander McQueen and Givenchy.

American designer, creative director, and musician whose work across Hood By Air, Helmut Lang, Diesel, Longchamp, Colmar A.G.E., his eponymous practice, and Anonymous Club has reshaped the relationship between luxury fashion, streetwear, queer nightlife, music, performance, gender, and collective authorship.

Liberian-American designer Telfar Clemens founded his eponymous New York label in 2005, building a radically inclusive, unisex wardrobe around familiar American clothing. Across runway collections, performance-led presentations, democratic accessories, uniforms, sportswear, and collaborations, Telfar has made accessibility and community central to luxury fashion. His practice encompasses the long-running TELFAR main line, the Shopping Bag, White Castle uniforms and capsules, Liberia's Olympic uniforms, and projects with UGG, Converse, and Moose Knuckles.

French designer Manfred Thierry Mugler founded his label in the 1970s and developed an unmistakable vocabulary of aerodynamic tailoring, corseted bodies, theatrical glamour, and science-fiction fantasy. His spectacular runway productions joined fashion, performance, celebrity, and image-making while celebrating transformation through exaggerated silhouette.

American designer Thom Browne began with five grey suits and a by-appointment New York shop, transforming the mid-century business uniform through cropped proportions and exacting construction. His practice expanded into womenswear and theatrical runway narratives populated by athletes, students, office workers, animals, and dream figures. Browne has repeatedly used the grey suit as both disciplined system and limitless storytelling device.

American designer and filmmaker Tom Ford transformed Gucci in the 1990s through a precise vocabulary of erotic glamour, then directed Yves Saint Laurent Rive Gauche while overseeing the Gucci Group. He founded his namesake house in 2005, extending his vision across menswear, womenswear, beauty, eyewear, and film. This profile attributes only collections designed during Ford's own tenures, separating his authorship from the houses that continued after him.
Designer and founder of Off-White whose career includes creative leadership at Louis Vuitton.
British designer whose work helped bring punk and new-wave style into fashion before expanding into historically informed tailoring, corsetry, environmental activism, and an influential global house.

Belgian designer and Antwerp Six member Walter Van Beirendonck has built an independent practice around explosive color, graphic symbolism, queer identity, political protest, and radically imaginative menswear. Alongside his namesake work, his 1990s W.&L.T. project brought cyberculture, rave energy, and mass-media experimentation into fashion.

American designer Willy Chavarria builds fashion around dignity, emotion, and the visibility of communities often excluded from luxury imagery. Drawing from his Mexican-American upbringing in California, Chicano style, queer culture, workwear, religion, and political struggle, he combines monumental tailoring and sportswear with deeply human casting. He launched his namesake collection in 2015 and has expanded its message from New York to Paris.
American designer, artist, and musician who founded Yeezy. His fashion work includes independent collections and former collaborations with Nike, Adidas, and Gap.

Japanese designer Yohji Yamamoto established his company in 1972 and presented in Paris in 1981. His work radically challenged Western ideals of glamour through black, asymmetry, generous volume, weathered textiles, and an insistence on space between garment and body. Across Yohji Yamamoto, Y's, and the Adidas partnership Y-3, he has sustained a poetic and rebellious approach to tailoring, movement, gender, and time.

French couturier Yves Saint Laurent succeeded Christian Dior at age 21 before founding his own house with Pierre Bergé in 1961. He transformed twentieth-century dress through the tuxedo, safari jacket, transparent blouse, trouser suit, and references spanning modern art and global cultural history. His Rive Gauche line made designer ready-to-wear central to modern fashion.

collections.name: Music
collections.description: Musical notation, instruments, and rhythmic graphic motifs turned garments and accessories into playful compositions.

collections.label: Schiaparelli
collections.name: Pagan
collections.description: Botanical forms, Botticelli references, and imagery of nature shaped an earthy counterpoint to Schiaparelli's more mechanical Surrealism.

collections.label: Schiaparelli
collections.name: Circus
collections.description: Acrobats, animals, spectacle, and trompe-l'œil transformed couture into a vivid Surrealist performance, including celebrated collaborations with Salvador Dalí.

credits.attribution_note: Founder and couturière; artist collaborations are described without assigning collection-level co-design credit.

collections.label: Schiaparelli
collections.name: Commedia dell'Arte
collections.description: Commedia dell'Arte characters and theatrical motifs extended Schiaparelli's practice of treating a couture collection as a complete narrative world.

collections.label: Gosha Rubchinskiy
collections.name: Empire of Evil
collections.description: Rubchinskiy’s debut staged post-Soviet youth, skate culture, and Russia’s sportswear fixation through confrontational bear-and-rifle graphics and a cast drawn from Moscow’s streets.

collections.label: Gosha Rubchinskiy
collections.description: Street-cast models evoked brand-hungry Russian youth of the early post-Soviet 1990s through counterfeit-like flag graphics, tracksuits, washed denim, workwear, and sheepskin outerwear.

collections.label: Gosha Rubchinskiy
collections.description: Soviet-era athletic uniforms and 1980s Olympic imagery were recast in high shorts, cinched track pants, striped vests, graphic knits, and deliberately awkward sportswear color.

collections.label: Gosha Rubchinskiy
collections.name: Kaliningrad
collections.description: A return to Russia paired regional street casting and recorded youth monologues with broadened tailoring and the debut of an Adidas Football collaboration ahead of the 2018 World Cup.

collections.label: Gosha Rubchinskiy
collections.name: Pitti Uomo
collections.description: Presented in a former Florence tobacco factory, the collection joined Pasolini-inspired tailoring with collaborations from Fila, Kappa, Sergio Tacchini, and Levi’s.

collections.label: Gosha Rubchinskiy
collections.name: Yekaterinburg
collections.description: Rubchinskiy’s final traditional seasonal runway explored uniforms, international youth solidarity, and 1990s Russia through hybrid construction and collaborations with Adidas, Burberry, Levi’s, Dr. Martens, and artist Erik Bulatov.

collections.label: Gosha Rubchinskiy
collections.name: St. Petersburg
collections.description: Football, late-Soviet rave culture, and nightlife converged in neon sportswear, mismatched tailoring, Adidas pieces, Stephen Jones hats, and Rubchinskiy’s first Burberry collaboration.

collections.label: Wales Bonner
collections.name: Ebonics
collections.description: Her graduate collection established a language of Black identity, European luxury, precise tailoring, and intimate adornment.

collections.label: Wales Bonner
collections.name: Malik
collections.description: A meditation on Black male representation that combined ceremonial elegance, sensuality, and exacting craft.

collections.label: Wales Bonner
collections.name: Spirituals
collections.description: A soulful study of faith, migration, and Black transatlantic style rendered through refined menswear.

collections.label: Wales Bonner
collections.name: Ezekiel
collections.description: Wales Bonner expanded her diasporic research through devotional imagery, tailoring, and richly symbolic embellishment.

collections.label: Wales Bonner
collections.name: Ecstatic Recital
collections.description: A poetic collection informed by spirituality, literary research, and the elegance of diasporic self-fashioning.

collections.label: Wales Bonner
collections.name: Lovers Rock
collections.description: The first chapter of a Caribbean trilogy explored 1970s London, lovers rock, and the exchange between Jamaican and British style.

collections.label: Wales Bonner
collections.name: Black Sunlight
collections.description: A liberated response to West African studio portraiture, balancing playful self-representation with disciplined tailoring.

collections.label: Wales Bonner
collections.name: Volta Jazz
collections.description: A collection shaped by Burkina Faso's musical and photographic culture, joining athletic ease to formal elegance.

collections.label: Wales Bonner
collections.description: The Spring/Summer 2024 menswear collection was titled Marathon.

collections.label: Wales Bonner
collections.name: Marathon
collections.description: Wales Bonner considered distance running as discipline, ritual, and a meeting point between athletic and ceremonial dress.

collections.label: Haider Ackermann
collections.description: Jewel-toned silks, leather, and suede were wrapped into long, lean silhouettes, balancing romantic drape with a newly masculine restraint.

collections.label: Haider Ackermann
collections.description: Languid silk pajamas, saturated gowns, plunging tuxedo shapes, and cropped leather jackets crystallized Ackermann's sensual, precisely disheveled early vocabulary.

collections.label: Berluti
collections.description: Ackermann's Berluti debut brought his languid tailoring and saturated color to the house's leather craft and luxury menswear vocabulary.

collections.label: Jean Paul Gaultier
collections.description: A one-season guest couture collection joined body-sharp tailoring and precise drape with Ackermann's restrained drama and command of color.

collections.label: Tom Ford
collections.description: Ackermann's Tom Ford debut recast the house's sensuality through sharp leather daywear, disciplined tailoring, and vivid evening color.

collections.label: Helmut Lang
collections.description: Lean tailoring, transparent layers, workwear, and restrained utility established Lang's influential alternative to decorative early-1990s fashion.

collections.label: Helmut Lang
collections.description: Military references, severe suiting, lingerie, and tactile contrasts made subversion feel precise, urban, and immediately wearable.

collections.label: Helmut Lang
collections.description: Protective outerwear, narrow tailoring, denim, and technical detail distilled late-1990s metropolitan dress into Lang's rigorous system.

collections.label: Helmut Lang
collections.description: Lang combined spare suiting, straps, sheer layers, and utilitarian garments in a wardrobe whose tension came from proportion and material rather than ornament.

collections.label: Helmut Lang
collections.description: At the turn of the millennium, Lang refined his vocabulary of technical utility, body-conscious layers, exact tailoring, and deliberately ordinary wardrobe pieces.

collections.label: Iris van Herpen
collections.name: Meta Morphism
collections.description: Meta Morphism considered identity and transformation through fluid construction, engineered surfaces, and the interdependence of physical and digital bodies.

collections.label: Iris van Herpen
collections.name: Architectonics
collections.description: Aquatic architecture, floating habitats, and oceanic systems informed layered geometries that treated the garment as a responsive structure around the body.

collections.label: Iris van Herpen
collections.name: Carte Blanche
collections.description: Created with freediver and filmmaker Julie Gautier, Carte Blanche placed couture underwater to connect movement, female resistance, and environmental perspective.

credits.attribution_note: Founder and couturière; the presentation film was created with Julie Gautier.

collections.label: Iris van Herpen
collections.name: Hybrid Show
collections.description: Five garments emerged from canvas-like installations in a hybrid fashion-and-art presentation exploring suspended time, sculpture, and bodily movement.

collections.label: Iris van Herpen
collections.name: Sympoiesis
collections.description: Bioluminescent algae, biomaterials, coral-like metal mesh, and ocean research framed couture as symbiotic creation across species and disciplines.

collections.label: Issey Miyake
collections.description: Miyake's early presentations proposed clothing as mobile architecture, joining Japanese textile knowledge to an experimental international wardrobe.

collections.label: Issey Miyake
collections.name: A-POC Prototype
collections.description: Miyake's continuing 'A Piece of Cloth' research explored how flat material could generate adaptable volume around many different bodies.

collections.label: Issey Miyake
collections.description: Heat-set pleating experiments placed permanent movement into finished garments, laying the technical foundation for Pleats Please.

collections.label: Pleats Please Issey Miyake
collections.name: Pleats Please
collections.description: The Pleats Please line made Miyake's garment-pleating innovation an accessible system: light, washable clothing engineered to move, fold, and travel.

collections.label: Issey Miyake
collections.description: Sculptural pleats and elastic geometries demonstrated how industrial process could produce both visual transformation and practical freedom.

collections.label: Issey Miyake
collections.name: Guest Artist: Cai Guo-Qiang
collections.description: Gunpowder drawings by Cai Guo-Qiang marked garments as part of Miyake's Guest Artist series, making collaboration and controlled accident integral to the clothes.

collections.label: Issey Miyake
collections.description: One of Miyake's final seasonal collections before handing womenswear to Naoki Takizawa consolidated decades of research into pleating, geometric volume, and bodily movement.

collections.label: Issey Miyake
collections.name: A-POC
collections.description: A-POC—A Piece of Cloth—used computer-guided industrial knitting to produce continuous tubes from which wearers could cut finished garments, rethinking production and authorship.

collections.label: Jean Paul Gaultier
collections.name: Les Tatouages
collections.description: Tattoo-print mesh, global references, exposed construction, and fluid casting made the body itself the collection's shifting surface.

collections.label: Jean Paul Gaultier
collections.description: Gaultier mixed exact tailoring, lingerie codes, street observation, and gender play in a characteristically inclusive fashion spectacle.

collections.label: Jean Paul Gaultier
collections.name: Couture Debut
collections.description: Gaultier's couture debut applied atelier technique to androgyny, denim, corsetry, and menswear, expanding the social and material vocabulary of haute couture.

collections.label: Jean Paul Gaultier
collections.description: Convertible garments, trompe-l'œil suiting, lingerie exposure, and Breton signatures joined technical ingenuity with deliberate provocation.

collections.label: Jean Paul Gaultier
collections.name: 50th Anniversary Farewell
collections.description: A career-spanning farewell transformed archival materials through upcycling, corsetry, tailoring, Breton stripes, performance, and an expansive multigenerational cast.

collections.label: Jil Sander
collections.description: Pure lines, immaculate fabric, and restrained tailoring expressed Sander's proposition that professional authority and sensuality could coexist without ornament.

collections.label: Jil Sander
collections.description: Long coats, lean suits, and quiet material richness positioned minimalism as a technically demanding form of luxury rather than absence.

collections.label: Jil Sander
collections.description: Sander refined the modern wardrobe through pale color, controlled transparency, and tailoring whose apparent simplicity depended on exceptional cut and cloth.

collections.label: Jil Sander
collections.description: Austere silhouettes and sumptuous surfaces balanced discipline with tactility at the height of Sander's influence on 1990s dress.

collections.label: Jil Sander
collections.description: The designer's final collection before her first departure distilled the house into precise suiting, advanced textiles, and calm, lucid color.

collections.label: Jil Sander
collections.description: Sander's first return to her house restored subtle proportion, fabric innovation, and the emotional force of restraint.

collections.label: Jil Sander
collections.description: Her second return revisited the disciplined wardrobe with crisp volume and vivid blocks of color, proving minimalism could be emphatic rather than neutral.

collections.label: Jil Sander
collections.description: Sander's final collection for her namesake house used monastic shapes, controlled geometry, and concentrated color as a quiet farewell.

collections.label: John Elliott
collections.description: Elliott's debut runway translated layered hoodies, engineered knits, distressed denim, and elongated basics into a focused Los Angeles luxury system.

collections.label: John Elliott
collections.description: Fabric development and military references expanded the label beyond foundational sportswear while preserving its precise, wearable layering.

collections.label: John Elliott
collections.description: Sun-washed color, athletic pieces, and lightweight layers refined Elliott's intersection of California ease and globally sourced material research.

collections.label: John Elliott
collections.name: Delirium
collections.description: A darker, psychologically charged collection placed distressed surfaces, enveloping layers, and technical outerwear against the label's athletic foundation.

collections.label: John Elliott
collections.name: Field Manual
collections.description: Travel and military utility informed modular outerwear, washed fabrics, tactical details, and the season's expanded approach to complete dressing.

collections.label: John Elliott
collections.description: Runway-scale layering brought Italian fabrication, American sportswear, and travel research together in the label's increasingly expansive wardrobe.

collections.label: John Elliott
collections.name: Leap of Faith
collections.description: A return to the runway framed risk and renewal through relaxed tailoring, technical layers, basketball-informed proportions, and sun-faded California color.

collections.label: John Elliott
collections.description: The label's mature vocabulary of engineered basics, denim, performance fabrics, and layered outerwear was presented as an adaptable contemporary uniform.

collections.label: Givenchy
collections.description: John Galliano’s final couture collection for Givenchy combined the house’s aristocratic codes with his theatrical historicism, romantic bias cutting, elaborate surface work, and a cast of defining 1990s models.

collections.label: Christian Dior
collections.description: John Galliano's Fall 2000 haute couture collection for Dior used theatrical styling and couture construction to transform historical and cultural references into runway spectacle.

collections.label: Christian Dior
collections.name: Egypt
collections.description: Inspired by Galliano’s travels through Egypt, this gilded couture fantasia translated pharaohs, deities, hieroglyphs, tomb paintings, and mummification into an elongated Sphinx silhouette using gold leaf, lapis tones, lamé, coral beading, monumental jewelry, and extreme headdresses.

collections.label: Christian Dior
collections.name: Dior 60th Anniversary
collections.description: Presented at the Orangerie of the Palace of Versailles for Dior’s 60th anniversary, Galliano’s collection transformed references to major painters and fashion history into an opulent couture procession celebrating the house’s legacy.

collections.label: Maison Margiela
collections.name: Artisanal
collections.description: John Galliano’s final Artisanal collection for Maison Margiela transformed Brassaï-inspired nocturnal Paris into theatrical couture through extreme corsetry, decayed surfaces, bias cutting, character-driven movement, and Pat McGrath’s porcelain-like makeup.

collections.label: JW Anderson
collections.name: Parties That Never Were
collections.description: A digital collection celebrating dressing as a mischievous act beyond barriers of gender and taste. Metallic surfaces, saturated color, cartoon imagery, elephant and pigeon motifs, playful bags, and clashing proportions turned memories of missed parties into an unabashed fantasy.

collections.label: Loewe
collections.name: A New Aesthetic
collections.description: For Loewe’s return to the runway, Anderson called for a creative reset. Black column dresses erupted into metal-supported geometric volumes, while contorted draping, sculpted breastplates, surreal heels, and everyday objects pushed provocation, sensuality, and movement into a new visual language.

collections.label: Loewe
collections.name: Nature as Artifice
collections.description: Anderson examined nature that already resembles design through the poisonous anthurium flower. Molded floral bodices, fiberglass and metal structures, pixelated garments, split-arm leather dresses, and deliberately unreal surfaces tested the boundary between the physical body and the digital image.

collections.label: JW Anderson
collections.description: The collection reworked familiar wardrobe pieces with exaggerated proportions and unexpected materials.

collections.label: Christian Dior
collections.name: Promenade
collections.description: Shown around a water-lily pond in the Tuileries, Anderson relaxed Dior’s structure into light, mobile clothes. A knitted Bar jacket, pleated-silk tailoring, Junon-derived patterns, balloon trousers, lace frock coats, denim, and raffia flowers framed dressing as a promenade through Parisian history.

collections.label: Christian Dior
collections.name: Do You Dare Enter the House of Dior?
collections.description: Anderson’s Dior womenswear debut placed the house archive in deliberate collision with his own instincts. Shrunken Bar jackets, winged Cigale-derived volumes, denim, capes, lace, tricorne hats, and princess motifs blurred decades while balancing Dior formality with everyday dressing.

collections.label: Undercover
collections.name: Paper Doll
collections.description: Flat, cut-paper ideas became garments through trompe-l'oeil construction and displaced details, balancing childhood craft with unsettling precision.

collections.label: Undercover
collections.name: SCAB
collections.description: A landmark Paris debut built from patched, distressed, and hand-worked garments that translated crust-punk codes into an obsessive couture-like system.

collections.label: Undercover
collections.name: But Beautiful II
collections.description: Handmade-looking plush forms, Patti Smith references, and fragile decoration turned damage and imperfection into one of Takahashi's defining expressions of beauty.

collections.label: Undercover
collections.name: Arts & Crafts
collections.description: Felt, embroidery, raw edges, and handcrafted assemblage proposed an intimate alternative to polished luxury while preserving Undercover's punk tension.

collections.label: Undercover
collections.name: The Greatest
collections.description: A title drawn from the label's own archive framed a collection of layered references, graphic interventions, and familiar Undercover ideas reactivated rather than nostalgically repeated.

collections.label: Undercover
collections.name: We Are Infinite
collections.description: A dual presentation with Takahiro Miyashita used adolescent archetypes, literary atmosphere, and intricate layering to imagine parallel tribes and identities.

collections.label: Undercover
collections.name: The New Warriors
collections.description: Inspired by The Warriors, Takahashi organized menswear into optimistic fictional gangs, each with distinct styling, graphics, and subcultural codes.

collections.label: Undercover
collections.description: Inspired by Wim Wenders's Perfect Days, the collection honored routine and ordinary life through domestic gestures, layered tailoring, and garments carrying scenes of daily existence.

collections.label: Junya Watanabe Comme des Garçons
collections.name: Techno Couture
collections.description: Watanabe transformed hand-sewn polyester chiffon into enormous honeycomb ruffs and ethereal volumes that could collapse flat for storage. The collection fused historical couture technique, Rembrandt-era silhouettes, and space-age synthetic material into one of his defining statements.

collections.label: Junya Watanabe Comme des Garçons
collections.name: Function and Practicality
collections.description: A landmark rain-soaked presentation that made material performance visible on the runway. Transformable dresses, waterproof skirts, attached wrap scarves, pleating, and futuristic headpieces joined advanced synthetic textiles to precise, functional pattern cutting.

collections.label: Junya Watanabe Comme des Garçons
collections.name: Classic Clothing, Interpreted
collections.description: Edwardian romance and classic tailoring were destabilized through raw hems, unraveling sleeves, rough tweeds, tartans, oversized bows, and punk-inflected Chanel references. Watanabe treated proper period clothing as material for reconstruction rather than nostalgia.

collections.label: Junya Watanabe Comme des Garçons
collections.name: Parachute
collections.description: Romantic floral dresses and cropped trousers were suspended and gathered with parachute webbing, straps, buckles, and integrated backpacks. Airy umbrella hats completed Watanabe’s improbable fusion of pastoral innocence, combat utility, and transformable construction.

collections.label: Junya Watanabe Comme des Garçons
collections.name: Army
collections.description: Models advanced like a battalion in army green as Watanabe rebuilt fatigues, camouflage, concert-shirt patchwork, lace, parkas, trenches, and tailcoats into an antiwar-inflected punk wardrobe. Electrical-tape masks, studs, and trailing straps sharpened its subversive force.

collections.label: Junya Watanabe
collections.name: Kashmir
collections.description: Led Zeppelin’s Kashmir launched a dark pilgrimage of futuristic travelers. Rebuilt motorcycle jackets, technical strapping, carabiners, mesh, protective masks, studded boots, leather pleating, and abstract down-filled buffers blended exploration gear with dystopian romance.

collections.label: Junya Watanabe
collections.name: Creating Objects, Not Clothes
collections.description: Watanabe’s geometric pattern cutting produced wearable sculpture from jutting triangles, curved tubes, scuba neoprene, origami-folded biker jackets, fractal denim, and deconstructed bouclé. Extreme black objects gradually resolved into recognizable garments without surrendering their strangeness.

collections.label: Junya Watanabe MAN
collections.description: A menswear collection combining formalwear with a punk sensibility.

collections.label: Pyer Moss
collections.description: Jean-Raymond's Fall 2017 Pyer Moss collection continued his dialogue between contemporary American dress, identity, and social observation.

collections.label: Pyer Moss
collections.description: Pyer Moss combined American sportswear with Jean-Raymond's socially engaged approach to storytelling and presentation.

collections.label: Pyer Moss
collections.name: American, Also. Lesson 1
collections.description: The first chapter of Pyer Moss's American, Also series began a sustained examination of Black American history, representation, and cultural authorship.

collections.label: Pyer Moss
collections.name: American, Also. Lesson 2
collections.description: The second chapter of Pyer Moss's American, Also series centered everyday Black American life and the history of the Negro Motorist Green Book, incorporating commissioned paintings by Derrick Adams.

collections.label: Pyer Moss
collections.name: Sister
collections.description: The final chapter of the American, Also trilogy honored Sister Rosetta Tharpe and the obscured Black roots of rock and roll through fashion, music, and a large-scale performance at Brooklyn's Kings Theatre.

collections.label: Dunhill
collections.description: Jones modernized British luxury through travel-informed sportswear, refined outerwear, and an ease grounded in masculine utility.

collections.label: Louis Vuitton
collections.description: His Vuitton debut connected the house’s travel heritage to light tailoring, technical fabric, and a globally observant wardrobe.

collections.label: Louis Vuitton x Supreme
collections.name: Louis Vuitton x Supreme
collections.description: The landmark Supreme collaboration collapsed a longstanding boundary between luxury heritage and New York skate culture.

collections.label: Dior Men
collections.description: Jones’s Dior debut placed a giant KAWS figure amid pale tailoring, couture-derived construction, floral surfaces, and relaxed menswear.

collections.label: Fendi
collections.description: Jones’s Fendi debut drew on Virginia Woolf’s Orlando and the Bloomsbury circle for a literary, gender-fluid couture procession.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: Highland Rape
collections.description: McQueen confronted the historical violence inflicted on Scotland through torn tartan, lace, and radically lowered tailoring.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: Dante
collections.description: A candlelit church presentation joined religious imagery, war photography, skeletal lace, and razor-sharp tailoring.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: It's a Jungle Out There
collections.description: Predator-prey imagery, horned styling, animal skins, and ferocious tailoring framed fashion as survival.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: La Poupée
collections.description: Inspired by Hans Bellmer's dolls, the show tested the boundaries between bodily restriction, distortion, and beauty.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: Joan
collections.description: Joan of Arc inspired armor-like tailoring and a fiery finale that fused martyrdom with defiant female power.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: No. 13
collections.description: A landmark Lee Alexander McQueen collection known for its theatrical runway presentation.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: What a Merry-Go-Round
collections.description: A dark fairground staged military precision, distressed finery, and macabre spectacle around a carousel.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: Voss
collections.description: A mirrored psychiatric ward forced the audience to confront itself before revealing a glass box of moths at the finale.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: The Widows of Culloden
collections.description: McQueen revisited Scottish history with romantic tartans, antlered silhouettes, and a spectral Kate Moss hologram.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: The Horn of Plenty
collections.description: A severe satire of fashion excess transformed refuse, historical silhouettes, and McQueen's own archive into grandeur.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: Plato's Atlantis
collections.description: McQueen imagined humanity evolving beneath rising seas in a digitally printed, technologically staged final runway collection.

collections.label: Hot Mess
collections.name: Debut Capsule
collections.description: Created with photographer Noah Dillon alongside their week-long Milk Studios installation, Hot Mess’s first clothing drop turned repurposed garments, appropriated typography, and youth-culture imagery into deliberately anti-fashion merchandise.

collections.label: Luka Sabbat x Monini
collections.name: SSENSE Exclusive Jewelry
collections.description: Designed with Italian jeweler Gianni Monini, this concise range translated flea-market biker jewelry and Sabbat’s childhood references into sterling-silver rings, necklaces, and bracelets with restrained stone accents.

collections.label: Sabbat x Related
collections.name: Haiti
collections.description: Luka and his father Clark Sabbat joined Related Garments for an underwear-and-socks collection honoring their Haitian heritage, using flag colors and revolutionary references while directing proceeds toward HELP’s educational work.

collections.label: Champion x Luka Sabbat
collections.name: 100 Years of Champion
collections.description: For Champion’s centenary, Sabbat worked with young creatives from New York nonprofit Art Start on a limited graphic for Reverse Weave hoodies and T-shirts celebrating imagination realized through teamwork.

collections.label: Hot Mess
collections.name: SSENSE Exclusives
collections.description: Sabbat and Noah Dillon expanded Hot Mess into an SSENSE-exclusive release of graphic T-shirts, shirts, and fleece pieces carrying subversive images and anti-establishment messages.

collections.label: Luka Sabbat for ABOUT YOU
collections.description: Sabbat’s first premium menswear collection drew on Japanese punk, heavy metal, cinema, and his personal wardrobe, using customizable patches across military outerwear, leather, denim, knitwear, and jersey basics.

collections.label: Marking Distance
collections.name: Debut Collection
collections.description: The label’s first full collection, designed by Sabbat and James Pierce, combined hand-distressed leather, waxed cotton, altered denim, uniform references, punk craft, cinematic fetish imagery, and removable custom hardware across 33 looks.

collections.label: Marking Distance
collections.description: The second Marking Distance lookbook developed its hand-worked language through distressed biker leather, waxed and overdyed cotton, hybrid denim, studded accessories, patched uniforms, and corroded surface treatments.

collections.label: Marking Distance
collections.description: Marking Distance’s publicly previewed third seasonal lookbook continues Sabbat and Pierce’s evolving ready-to-wear project through experimental construction, distressed surfaces, graphic storytelling, and subcultural references.

collections.label: Perry Ellis
collections.name: Grunge
collections.description: Jacobs translated thrifted flannel, floral dresses, and layered youth culture into luxury fashion, losing his Perry Ellis position but changing the decade.

collections.label: Marc Jacobs
collections.description: Downtown eclecticism, vintage references, and precise styling demonstrated Jacobs’s talent for turning cultural mood into desirable character.

collections.label: Louis Vuitton
collections.description: The Richard Prince collaboration combined nurse imagery, painterly monograms, and elaborate accessories in Jacobs’s art-driven Vuitton era.

collections.label: Louis Vuitton
collections.description: Jacobs’s all-black farewell revisited escalators, fountains, elevators, and showgirl spectacle from his sixteen years defining Vuitton ready-to-wear.

collections.label: Marc Jacobs
collections.description: Gothic scale, towering platforms, craft, and dramatic volume produced an imposing meditation on beauty and subculture.

collections.label: Marine Serre
collections.name: Futurewear
collections.description: Following her LVMH Prize win, Serre joined crescent-moon bodysuits, protective sportswear, and regenerated materials into an urgent post-apocalyptic wardrobe.

collections.label: Marine Serre
collections.name: Marée Noire
collections.description: Marée Noire imagined ecological crisis through oil-dark surfaces, masks, regenerated textiles, and resilient hybrid clothing.

collections.label: Marine Serre
collections.name: Core
collections.description: A film-led collection centered families and communities wearing regenerated household textiles, tailoring, denim, and the moon motif.

collections.label: Marine Serre
collections.name: State of Soul
collections.description: A public-facing presentation expanded regenerated couture, sportswear, and diverse casting into an argument for fashion as collective practice.

collections.label: Marine Serre
collections.description: At the Monnaie de Paris, Serre infiltrated bourgeois archetypes with regenerated materials, feminist symbolism, and her own crescent currency.

collections.label: Maison Martin Margiela
collections.description: The debut established Tabi boots, exposed linings, distressed surfaces, and collective anonymity in a raw Paris presentation.

collections.label: Maison Martin Margiela
collections.description: A legendary playground show in a working-class Paris neighborhood invited local children and dismantled the distance between fashion spectacle and ordinary life.

collections.label: Maison Martin Margiela
collections.name: Stockman
collections.description: Dress forms, basting, shoulder pads, and unfinished structures exposed the tools by which idealized fashion bodies are manufactured.

collections.label: Maison Martin Margiela
collections.description: Flat garments, extreme scale, and conceptual pattern cutting challenged the assumption that clothes must resolve conventionally around the body.

collections.label: Maison Martin Margiela
collections.description: The house’s twentieth-anniversary show revisited masks, trompe-l’oeil, wigs, repurposed objects, and anonymous collective performance near the end of Margiela’s tenure.

collections.label: Martine Rose
collections.description: Rose distorted familiar football, club, and office archetypes through twisted shirting, broad trousers, and intensely specific casting.

collections.label: Martine Rose
collections.description: A London presentation fused corporate clothing, subcultural swagger, and awkwardly persuasive proportion into a portrait of contemporary masculinity.

collections.label: Martine Rose
collections.description: Domestic interiors and distorted everyday dressing explored privacy, exposure, and the peculiar glamour of ordinary masculine clothes.

collections.label: Martine Rose
collections.description: Shown under the Vauxhall arches, compressed silhouettes, club energy, and community casting reasserted the label after its runway pause.

collections.label: Martine Rose
collections.description: Character-led styling and deliberately unsettled proportions continued Rose’s study of how real people make clothing culturally legible.

collections.label: 1017 ALYX 9SM
collections.description: Industrial buckles, technical fabrication, and severe utility expressed Williams’s fusion of subculture and engineered luxury.

collections.label: 1017 ALYX 9SM
collections.description: Hardware-driven tailoring and protective outerwear refined the label’s controlled, urban system.

collections.label: Givenchy
collections.description: Williams’s Givenchy debut introduced sharp hardware, compressed silhouettes, and pragmatic luxury through a lookbook made during the pandemic.

collections.label: Givenchy
collections.description: Layered denim, tailoring, and aggressive accessories pushed his dialogue between American street culture and Parisian house technique.

collections.label: Givenchy
collections.description: Williams’s final Givenchy collection clarified his signatures in lean tailoring, technical outerwear, and metal-accented accessories.

collections.label: Bottega Veneta
collections.description: Blazy’s debut began with deceptively simple clothing—including leather engineered to look like denim—and centered craft in motion.

collections.label: Bottega Veneta
collections.description: Everyday characters, fluid tailoring, and material illusion expanded his idea of the Italian wardrobe as a moving social panorama.

collections.label: Bottega Veneta
collections.description: Travel, transformation, and extraordinary leather workmanship created clothing that balanced childlike imagination with adult precision.

collections.label: Bottega Veneta
collections.description: Blazy’s final Bottega runway placed expressive characters around animal-shaped chairs, completing his trilogy about everyday wonder and craft.

collections.label: Chanel
collections.description: Blazy’s Chanel debut reanimated house codes through movement, material experimentation, and a less fixed idea of the Chanel woman.

collections.label: Prada
collections.description: A defining chapter of Prada's pretty-ugly revolution, using autumnal off-colors and deliberately awkward references to challenge conventional taste.

collections.label: Prada
collections.description: Art Nouveau fairies, wood-nymph prints, curving knits, and grounded platform footwear expressed Miuccia Prada's search for a new creativity.

collections.label: Miu Miu
collections.description: A romantic but provocative sixties silhouette combined high collars, rosettes, abbreviated skirts, and strategically exposed skin.

collections.label: Prada
collections.description: Prada reconsidered femininity through emphatic proportions, knitwear, and a provocative focus on the bust and the body.

collections.label: Miu Miu
collections.description: Narrow plaid tailoring, tiny skirts, knit socks, fur, and locked buckles mixed sixties youthfulness with Prada's characteristically perverse edge.

collections.label: Prada
collections.description: A Miuccia Prada collection drawing on 1950s automobile imagery.

collections.label: Prada
collections.description: Monumental mural imagery, jeweled sportswear, and visible bras turned the runway into a forceful argument about women, art, and public space.

collections.label: Prada
collections.description: A synthetic, pastel vision of the future used double-faced jersey, abbreviated proportions, and deliberately uncanny sweetness.

collections.label: Miu Miu
collections.description: Denim, military tailoring, tapestry, velvet, and eveningwear formed an eclectic meditation on nobility, scarcity, and dressing with what remains.

collections.label: Prada
collections.description: Miuccia Prada's final solo womenswear show for the house examined strength, glamour, fringe, and the tension between protection and exposure.

collections.label: Miu Miu
collections.description: Presented at a Paris racecourse, the collection played with conservatism through roomy shorts, elongated collars, platform shoes, glamour, and fun.

collections.label: Miu Miu
collections.description: The viral collection cut corporate uniforms into raw-edged micro proportions, transforming familiar office clothes into a post-lockdown generational statement.

collections.label: Miu Miu
collections.description: An inquiry into looking and being looked at used cardigans, cabans, visible tights, briefs, and deliberately unsettled ideas of elegance.

collections.label: Kenzo
collections.name: Kenzo Debut
collections.description: Nigo's Kenzo debut joined Japanese denim, post-Ivy uniforms, workwear, and respectful study of Kenzo Takada's archive in the Galerie Vivienne.

collections.label: Kenzo
collections.description: Mod culture, Beatles references, Japanese tailoring, kimono construction, and English country codes marked a more personal chapter in Nigo's Kenzo tenure.

collections.label: Kenzo
collections.name: Class of 2023
collections.description: A graduation theme unified Japanese denim, naval dress, school uniforms, Americana, and revived Kenzo archive graphics into a cross-generational wardrobe.

collections.label: Kenzo
collections.description: City-pop memory connected Japanese tailoring, hakama-derived proportion, denim, and Kenzo archive motifs, with graphic contributions from Verdy.

credits.attribution_note: Kenzo artistic director; Verdy contributed collection graphics.

collections.label: Balmain
collections.description: Rousteing's Balmain debut translated the house's military structure into opulent, hyper-fitted leather, gold embroidery, and Fabergé-like surface work.

collections.label: Balmain
collections.description: Safari and utility references met graphic weaving, rope, and commanding shoulders as Rousteing broadened the public image of his Balmain Army.

collections.label: Balmain x H&M
collections.name: Balmain x H&M
collections.description: A mass-market capsule translated Rousteing's embellished jackets, body-conscious silhouettes, and military glamour for a dramatically wider audience.

collections.label: Balmain
collections.description: Fluid draping, cutaway knitwear, safari palettes, and intricate evening surfaces loosened the armor of Rousteing's earlier Balmain vocabulary.

collections.label: Balmain
collections.description: A celebration of confidence and pop-cultural scale combined saturated color, graphic tailoring, and the designer's increasingly personal public narrative.

collections.label: Balmain
collections.description: Presented after Rousteing revealed his recovery from severe burns, the collection treated bandaging, protection, exposure, and healing through wrapped and armored silhouettes.

collections.label: Balmain
collections.description: A love letter to Bordeaux and Rousteing's adoptive mother Lydia transformed vineyard grapes, gingham picnics, trench coats, and childhood memories into Balmain spectacle.

collections.label: Balmain
collections.description: Rousteing's final runway chapter returned to the ballroom of his 2011 debut, replacing early rigidity with shells, wood, draped silk, and a softer idea of opulence.

collections.label: Billionaire Boys Club
collections.description: The early BBC/Icecream universe joined Nigo’s Japanese production knowledge to Pharrell’s music, skate, space, and prep references.

collections.label: Chanel
collections.name: Chanel Pharrell
collections.description: A unisex capsule translated Pharrell’s personal Chanel vocabulary into hoodies, jewelry, loafers, robes, and vivid color.

collections.label: Louis Vuitton
collections.description: American Western imagery, workwear, and collaboration with Indigenous artists expanded the house’s travel narrative.

collections.label: Louis Vuitton
collections.description: Pharrell’s Louis Vuitton debut transformed the Pont Neuf into a celebration of community, Damier, tailoring, and Black cultural visibility.

collections.label: Louis Vuitton
collections.name: Remember the Future
collections.description: Pharrell Williams and Nigo co-designed a collection shaped by their shared history, Japanese craft and workwear references, Louis Vuitton travel codes, and decades of creative exchange.

credits.attribution_note: Louis Vuitton men's creative director and co-designer.
Guest co-designer and longtime creative partner.

collections.label: Louis Vuitton
collections.description: A global diplomatic wardrobe used skin-tone gradients, travel tailoring, and collective spectacle to argue for connection across difference.

collections.label: Celine
collections.description: Disciplined outerwear, leather, knitwear, and exact proportions extended Philo's proposition for an intelligent, functional modern wardrobe.

collections.label: Celine
collections.name: Celine Debut
collections.description: Philo's Celine runway debut reset luxury womenswear through clean neutrals, assured daywear, precise separates, and a pragmatic form of sensuality.

collections.label: Celine
collections.description: Unfinished silks, intuitive draping, relaxed confidence, and fur-lined sandals moved Philo's work beyond reductive minimalism toward tactile eccentricity.

collections.label: Celine
collections.description: Brassaï-inspired brushstroke graphics, asymmetric pleating, strong color, and energized movement made this a defining expression of Philo's instinctive modernism.

collections.label: Celine
collections.description: Elongated fit-and-flare silhouettes, layered trousers, practical sandals, and unexpected lightness grew from Philo's lived, wearer-centered design process.

collections.label: Valentino
collections.description: Piccioli’s first solo ready-to-wear collection joined medieval and punk references with lyrical dresses and a newly individual house voice.

collections.label: Valentino
collections.description: Diverse casting, saturated couture color, and expansive volume made beauty feel both elevated and socially open.

collections.label: Valentino
collections.name: Pink PP
collections.description: An almost entirely hot-pink and black environment used radical chromatic reduction to focus attention on silhouette, identity, and individual presence.

collections.label: Valentino
collections.description: Piccioli’s final ready-to-wear collection for Valentino explored the body through intricate cutwork, monochrome surfaces, and lightness.

collections.label: Balenciaga
collections.name: The Heartbeat
collections.description: Piccioli’s Balenciaga debut reconciled Cristóbal’s architectural volume with his own humanistic color, elegance, and emotional clarity.

collections.label: Raf Simons
collections.name: Riot! Riot! Riot!
collections.description: Raf Simons returned from a one-year sabbatical with a landmark collection staged in a smoke-filled warehouse. Oversized, layered silhouettes and youth-subculture references framed clothing as protection, identity, and revolt.

collections.label: Raf Simons
collections.name: Nightmares and Dreams
collections.description: Raf Simons explored adolescent dreams and nightmares through distressed, oversized tailoring and knitwear in a labyrinthine set, accompanied by Angelo Badalamenti discussing his work with David Lynch.

collections.label: Raf Simons
collections.description: Raf Simons presented his first namesake runway show in New York, combining an immigrant’s view of the city with punk-inflected graphics, oversized outerwear, and an argument for fearlessness.

collections.label: Raf Simons
collections.description: A Raf Simons menswear collection presented in Paris, extending the designer’s exploration of youth culture through elongated proportions, graphic layering, and subcultural references.

collections.label: Prada
collections.description: Prada Spring/Summer 2024 womenswear, jointly designed by co-creative directors Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons. The collection explored freedom of the body through lightweight dresses, reworked menswear silhouettes, and reinterpreted archival designs.

collections.label: Luar
collections.description: The last documented Luar runway season before an extended pause, continuing Lopez's collision of downtown experimentation, dramatic silhouette, and the social codes of dressing up.

collections.label: Luar
collections.description: An early chapter in Luar's documented runway archive, bringing Lopez's subversive treatment of proportion, gender, and New York street language into a sharply personal ready-to-wear proposition.

collections.label: Luar
collections.description: Luar's emphatic return to New York Fashion Week introduced the sculptural, circular-handled Ana bag. Named for Lopez's mother and grandmother, the accessory distilled family memory, aspiration, and downtown glamour into the object that helped transform the label's reach.

collections.label: Luar
collections.name: Calle Pero Elegante
collections.description: Streetwise but elegant, the collection sharpened Luar's tailoring and accessories while treating glamour as a language built in community rather than granted by conventional luxury institutions.

collections.label: Luar
collections.name: La Alta Gama
collections.description: A study of 'high class' aspiration filtered through the resourcefulness and presentation rituals of Lopez's Dominican-American upbringing, combining exaggerated tailoring, evening drama, and the cultivated swagger of neighborhood elegance.

collections.label: Luar
collections.name: Deceptionista
collections.description: An autobiographical meditation on metrosexuality and the strategies queer men used to navigate masculinity. Elizabethan volume, animal textures, narrow silhouettes, and ornamental beauty marked the runway, which also introduced Luar Basics and a partnership with Moose Knuckles.

collections.label: Luar
collections.name: Socorro
collections.description: Named in homage to Lopez's mother, 'Socorro' drew on a scene in El Hoyo in the Dominican Republic where street revelry and outdoor worship faced one another. Streamlined tailoring, convertible garments, church references, and hedonistic tension shaped the collection.

collections.label: Luar
collections.name: El Pato
collections.description: Lopez reclaimed 'pato'—both Spanish for duck and a homophobic slur in parts of Latin America—as a defiant queer emblem. Feathers, sculpted gestures, asymmetric tailoring, and 1980s maximalism paid homage to the flamboyant designers and queer figures he admired.

collections.label: Luar
collections.name: En Boca Quedó
collections.description: Staged in Rockefeller Plaza, the collection brought Luar's downtown community into one of New York's most visible civic stages. Lopez answered the pressure of mainstream attention with corsetry, high-impact tailoring, theatrical accessories, and the energy of a public spectacle.

collections.label: Luar
collections.description: A love letter to Dominican carnival and the resilience carried through its craft traditions. Working with artisans and references including Los Pintaos, Lopez paired severe elongated tailoring with vivid painted surfaces, amber, larimar, and contemporary interpretations of ancestral celebration.

collections.label: Comme des Garçons
collections.name: Destroy
collections.description: Kawakubo's Paris breakthrough used black, asymmetry, holes, and distressed knitwear to overturn prevailing Western ideas of luxury and finish.

collections.label: Comme des Garçons
collections.name: Body Meets Dress, Dress Meets Body
collections.description: Rei Kawakubo challenged conventional silhouettes using asymmetrical padded forms.

collections.label: Comme des Garçons
collections.name: Transcending Gender
collections.description: Hybrid tailoring and deliberately unstable gender codes continued Kawakubo's dismantling of fixed categories of dress and identity.

collections.label: Comme des Garçons
collections.name: Broken Bride
collections.description: Fragmented bridal references turned romance, ceremony, and incompletion into an unsettled study of beauty.

collections.label: Comme des Garçons
collections.name: 2 Dimensions
collections.description: Flat felt silhouettes reduced clothing toward two dimensions, turning the runway into a moving sequence of paper-doll forms.

collections.label: Comme des Garçons
collections.name: White Drama
collections.description: An all-white procession abstracted the rituals marking birth, marriage, death, and transcendence into sculptural form.

collections.label: Comme des Garçons
collections.name: Not Making Clothes
collections.description: Kawakubo abandoned conventional garments for eighteen abstract constructions that asked where clothing ends and pure creation begins.

collections.label: Comme des Garçons
collections.name: The Ceremony of Separation
collections.description: Monumental lace forms in black, white, and gold staged mourning as a slow ritual between the living and the dead.

collections.label: Comme des Garçons
collections.name: Blood and Roses
collections.description: A nearly all-red sequence transformed roses, blood, violence, and historical dress into an unnerving struggle toward beauty.

collections.label: Comme des Garçons
collections.name: The Future of Silhouette
collections.description: Bulbous forms made from wadding, paper, lace, and recycled material proposed silhouette as an open field beyond ordinary garment construction.

collections.label: Comme des Garçons
collections.name: Invisible Clothes
collections.description: Enormous structures swallowed the body while asserting an unmistakable female presence, challenging visibility and the definition of clothing itself.

collections.label: Comme des Garçons
collections.name: Anger
collections.description: Rei Kawakubo described the collection as an expression of anger at the state of the world and at herself.

collections.label: Rick Owens
collections.name: Dustulator
collections.description: Owens refined his glamorous post-apocalyptic vocabulary through sweeping volumes, washed surfaces, and sculptural leather.

collections.label: Rick Owens
collections.name: Crust
collections.description: Layered knits, elongated proportions, and distressed textures gave Owens's menswear an austere nomadic force.

collections.label: Rick Owens
collections.name: Limo
collections.description: Monumental outerwear and disciplined draping recast Owens's underground signatures with stately restraint.

collections.label: Rick Owens
collections.name: Mountain
collections.description: Protective layers and imposing footwear turned the male silhouette into a severe, mobile monument.

collections.label: Rick Owens
collections.name: Vicious
collections.description: A presentation performed by four step teams that challenged conventional runway casting and beauty standards.

collections.label: Rick Owens
collections.name: Mastodon
collections.description: Ecological anxiety took form in Jurassic parkas, primordial layers, and Owens's apocalyptic romanticism.

collections.label: Rick Owens
collections.name: Cyclops
collections.description: A narrow-focus monster inspired radical proportion, suspended geometry, and a deliberately confrontational runway moment.

collections.label: Rick Owens
collections.name: Dirt
collections.description: Owens explored migration, ceremony, and raw physicality through trailing layers and earthbound tones.

collections.label: Rick Owens
collections.name: Babel
collections.description: Constructivist scaffolding, sharp tailoring, and wearable structures balanced order against chaos.

collections.label: Rick Owens
collections.name: Tecuatl
collections.description: Owens connected his Mexican heritage to glam, geometry, and ceremonial severity in a deeply personal collection.

collections.label: Rick Owens
collections.name: Strobe
collections.description: An extreme play of shoulders, transparency, and elongated form delivered glamour as both armor and provocation.

collections.label: A-COLD-WALL*
collections.description: Ross continued A-COLD-WALL*'s investigation of industrial Britain, class, protection, and architectural form through technical materials and structured layering.

collections.label: A-COLD-WALL*
collections.description: Samuel Ross examined social mobility and the built environment through industrial construction, protective layers, distressed surfaces, and a performance that physically broke apart the show's set.

collections.label: A-COLD-WALL*
collections.description: A-COLD-WALL* translated industrial surfaces, functional clothing, and social architecture into a rigorous Fall 2020 menswear system.

collections.label: A-COLD-WALL*
collections.name: A Material Study for Social Architecture
collections.description: Presented at Printworks in London, the collection developed Ross's study of social architecture through material experimentation, workwear-derived forms, tailoring, and industrial references.

collections.label: A-COLD-WALL*
collections.description: Ross refined A-COLD-WALL*'s material-led vocabulary through modular construction, utility, and a continuing study of the relationship between clothing and environment.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: The Ice Queen and Her Court
collections.description: Regal silhouettes, intricate surfaces, and icy romance established Burton's ability to sustain spectacle through exquisite handwork.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: Debut
collections.description: Burton's first runway collection as creative director carried McQueen's exacting craft forward with a softer, nature-bound femininity of her own.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: Gaia
collections.description: Oceanic ruffles, coral forms, shells, and body-enclosing headpieces imagined women as powerful creatures of the natural world.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: The Honeycomb
collections.description: Beekeeper veils, honeycomb structures, and wasp-waisted tailoring made maternity, danger, and generative female power inseparable.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.description: A dark folkloric landscape of feathers, fur, moonlit embroidery, and protective silhouettes drew power from the British countryside.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.description: Seafaring histories, shipwrecked finery, and delicate botanical embroideries joined romance to the toughness of women who survive.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.description: Butterflies, beetles, flora, and found natural specimens informed a collection about transformation, preservation, and female strength.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.description: Burton centered the collective labor of the McQueen atelier, using flax, endangered crafts, and handwork rooted in British landscape and community.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.name: Anemones
collections.description: Crushed anemone imagery and water motifs expressed healing and renewal through rigorous tailoring and expansive floral gowns.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.description: Anatomy, cut, and the slash became a precise study of construction that reaffirmed Burton's mastery near the close of her McQueen tenure.

collections.label: Alexander McQueen
collections.description: Sarah Burton's final collection as creative director of Alexander McQueen.

collections.label: Givenchy
collections.description: The collection focused on cut, proportion, and tailoring.

collections.label: Givenchy
collections.description: Burton's second Givenchy runway deepened her sensual, woman-centered vocabulary through sculpted tailoring, exposed construction, and confident eveningwear.

collections.label: Hood By Air
collections.name: Prophets and Fetishists
collections.description: Hood By Air’s breakout New York runway fused a distant-future mood with streetwear, fetish codes, neoprene, aggressive graphics, and sculptural cut-and-sew garments. A$AP Rocky closed the smoke-and-laser presentation, marking HBA’s transition from cult graphic label to a new kind of designer house.

collections.label: Hood By Air
collections.description: Oliver made statements about gender, power, class, beauty, and commerce through oversized sports jerseys, bruise graphics, grommeted leather, bondage-inflected construction, and influential zip-detailed denim. A forceful ballroom performance transformed the finale into a declaration of HBA’s community and cultural source.

collections.label: Hood By Air
collections.name: Human Evolution
collections.description: Oliver treated categorization itself as a threat, hybridizing khakis, button-downs, puffers, sweaters, and T-shirts until familiar wardrobe staples appeared alien. Distorted faces, ambiguous bodies, and liminal silhouettes framed human evolution as a refusal of fixed identity.

collections.label: Hood By Air
collections.description: Presented across New York and Paris, the collection dismantled machismo through hybrid suits, jumpsuits, deconstructed shirting, transparent restraint devices, and orthopedic imagery. Oliver used restriction and vulnerability to challenge conventional ideas of masculine power.

collections.label: Hood By Air
collections.name: Pilgrimage
collections.description: Titled Pilgrimage, the collection explored transience, transmigration, and bodies treated as cargo. Patent-leather puffers, baggage-tagged shoes, plastic-wrapped bustiers, waders, dislocated sleeves, and luggage forms carried political undertones about displacement while demonstrating Oliver’s growing technical confidence.

collections.label: Hood By Air
collections.name: Self-Obsessed
collections.description: A Paris meditation on self-worship filtered old-Hollywood glamour, toddler dressing, and bodily control through partitioned garments, trailing trains, pleated culottes, padlocked pacifiers, and slashed silhouettes. The work treated clothing as philosophy in transition rather than stable menswear.

collections.label: Hood By Air
collections.name: Galvanize
collections.description: Drawing on Oliver’s Caribbean childhood and school uniforms worn amid unequal living conditions, Galvanize radically chopped, suspended, and reassembled denim, striped knits, skirts, dresses, and institutional dress. Gender was treated as secondary to membership in the HBA family.

collections.label: Hood By Air
collections.name: Wench
collections.description: Hood By Air shared billing with Wench, Oliver and Arca’s musical project, in a subversive take on tour merchandise.
